title: Four motives
hook: wrongdoing comes from desire, hate, delusion and fear

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sigala's bow, and your line, six directions. Who did you honor? Today closes a week, and the Buddha asks Sigala to look at why people go wrong. Day five hundred sixty-seven.

A referee calls a foul on the visiting team that wasn't a foul. Why? Maybe he likes the home team. Maybe he can't stand the visiting coach. Maybe he just didn't see it clearly. Or maybe forty thousand people were screaming, and he was afraid. Four possible reasons, and the same bad call. Before the Buddha explains the six directions to Sigala, he names exactly these four. Today: four motives.
screen: `A BAD CALL.` → `LIKING, DISLIKE, CONFUSION, FEAR.` → `THE SAME FOUL.`

segments.voice: In the Sigalovada the Buddha says a wise person does no evil from four motives. From desire. From hate. From delusion. From fear. The Pali calls them agati, literally not-going, wrong courses: four ways the mind goes off the road. Desire bends you toward what you want or who you like. Hate bends you against someone. Delusion means you simply don't see clearly. And fear bends you toward whatever keeps you safe. Notice that last one. Many lists of wrongdoing stop at greed, hate and delusion. This one adds fear, and that feels very true. A lot of harm isn't done out of malice at all. It's done by someone who was afraid to speak up, or afraid to lose a job, or afraid of a crowd. Then the Buddha puts it in verse. Whoever goes against the Dhamma from desire, hate, fear or delusion, his good name fades, like the moon in the waning half of the month. Whoever doesn't, his good name grows, like the moon in the waxing half. Two pictures, one shrinking, one filling. And the verse is about reputation, which was something Sigala, a young householder, would care about. Later Buddhist tradition takes these four as the classic biases a judge or a ruler must avoid. Look back at this week: chosen, not born; what I trust; well proclaimed; the marks of kindness; a protective chant; six directions; and now four reasons a good person might still make a bad call.
screen: `AGATI: FOUR WRONG COURSES.` · `DESIRE, HATE, DELUSION, FEAR.` · `FEAR IS ON THE LIST.` · `THE WANING MOON, THE WAXING MOON.` · then, large: `FOUR MOTIVES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and recall one recent decision you're not proud of. Small is fine: a sharp word, a corner cut, a silence when you should have spoken. Hold it gently. Then ask which motive was at work. Wanting something? Disliking someone? Not seeing clearly? Or fear? Don't judge yourself. Just name it, the way you'd name a bird you spotted. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Four motives. In DN 31: desire, hate, delusion and fear, the four wrong courses that lead good people into bad acts. Today's word.
Your line: four motives. Today, before one important choice, check the four: am I leaning from wanting, dislike, confusion, or fear? Day five hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often present the four agati as a checklist for fairness, and in Buddhist countries they have been cited as biases that judges, monastic elders and rulers must avoid.

pairs: the motive many lists leave out

myth: the Sigalovada lists only greed, hate and delusion as motives
it lists four: desire, hate, delusion and fear.

fork.setup: a referee makes a bad call because forty thousand fans are screaming at him. which of the four motives is at work?
fork.reveal: fear. the Sigalovada names it alongside desire, hate and delusion as a reason good people do wrong.

original.note: Pali agati: wrong course, literally not-going. the four are chanda, dosa, moha and bhaya.

trapdoor: what you thought: wrongdoing comes from bad intentions.
what it means: the Sigalovada names four motives, and one of them is simply fear.
what a scholar hears: the four agati (chanda, dosa, moha, bhaya) recur in the Anguttara (e.g. AN 4.17–20) and became a standard list of judicial bias in Buddhist legal and monastic thought.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta), the four agati and the moon verse

notes: DN 31 paraphrased. Confirm the order (chanda, dosa, moha, bhaya) and the moon verse.
